world.bio: I'm Priya Nair, forty-two, a family law solicitor in a small practice off Upper Street in Islington. I handle custody disputes, mostly, and a fair amount of divorce paperwork. I keep a box of tissues and a bowl of clementines on my desk because I have found that people can usually say the hard thing if they are holding something. My mother lives in Leeds and has had two falls this year; the family cannot agree on whether she should move south. At home, a kitchen extension is six weeks behind schedule and my son has discovered chess and beats me every time.
skills_assets: Fifteen years in family law, with a focus on child arrangements, contact disputes and financial remedy
A client list of around forty live cases, mostly separating parents in north London
Experience drafting consent orders, parenting plans and witness statements
Contacts with two barristers' chambers, a mediator, and a child psychologist who often acts as an expert witness
A Law Society Children Panel membership
A good ear for tone; she can tell within a minute whether a parent is describing a child or a grievance
A tiny box-room office with a window onto a plane tree

projects.name: Mum's move
projects.text: Mum is eighty-one and lives alone in a terraced house in Headingley. She has fallen twice this year, once in the kitchen and once on the stairs, and both times lay for a while before the neighbour came. My brother Anil says she should come to him in Reading; my sister Meena says she should stay put; I'm in the middle. Mum says she will go nowhere, thank you very much. We have a family video call every Sunday that ends in silence.

projects.name: Kitchen extension
projects.text: The builders were meant to finish by early August. We are now in October and the roof is on but the floor is still plywood. We have been washing up in the bathroom basin. My husband Dev has a spreadsheet. I have a headache.

projects.name: Pro bono Tuesday clinic
projects.text: Every second Tuesday evening I do a free advice clinic at a community centre in Finsbury Park. It is the part of my week where I feel most like the reason I became a lawyer.

notes.text: Court at 10, a contact dispute where both parents genuinely love the child and genuinely hate each other. I watched the father's hands during cross-examination. They did not stop shaking. At lunch I ate a clementine in the toilets and told myself I was fine.
Zain beat me at chess in nine moves. He is eight. He explained, with great patience, what I had done wrong, then asked if I wanted to play again. I said yes. He won in seven.

Rang Mum. She was out of breath. She said she'd been on the stairs. I asked if she'd been using the rail. She said she's not an invalid. I said I know. She said then stop asking. I stopped, and then asked again, in a different tone, and she hung up.
Builder says the plasterer can't come until the twenty-eighth. Dev made a graph of delays. It looks like a downward spiral. I told him it is the shape of my life and he laughed, which was nice.

Anil rang, calling me 'the rational one'. Which means he wants me to talk Mum into Reading. I said I won't force her. He said somebody has to. I said that sentence is how most of my clients end up in my office.

Late meeting with a client who wants to move abroad with her daughter. Her ex says no. I spent two hours explaining that the court cares about the child's relationship with both parents, not about who is nicer. She wept. I handed her a clementine.
Northern line stuck between Angel and Old Street for twenty minutes. A man beside me was reading a chess book, upside down. I almost said something but did not.

Free clinic tonight. A mother asked whether she could stop her ex taking the kids to his new partner's house. I explained what the court would actually look at. She said, 'No one's ever told me it that clearly.' I nearly cried on the bus home.

Meena sent a spreadsheet of care homes in Leeds. Every one has a pastel brochure and a smiling resident. I closed the file. I'd like, just once, for a hard decision in my family to be as simple as a statute.

messages.text:
Anil: She needs to move, Priya. Another fall and it's a hip.
Me: She's capable and she hates being managed.
Anil: Capable people fall too.
Me: I know. I know.

Dev: Plasterer's back on the 28th, apparently.
Me: Apparently.
Dev: I've bought paper plates.
Me: You're a hero.

Meena: Did you see my spreadsheet?
Me: Yes. Impressive.
Meena: And?
Me: Mum won't read it, Meena.

Zain: Mum, I'm in the school chess club!
Me: Of course you are.
Zain: Will you come to the tournament?
Me: I'll sit in the front row and look nervous.

Mum: I was out in the garden today, and I'm perfectly well.
Me: I'm glad.
Mum: You don't have to ring so often.
Me: I like ringing.

calendar.event: Family video call about Mum, 6 p.m.

relations.about: Eighty-one, lives alone in Leeds, has fallen twice this year.
Brother in Reading, wants Mum to move.

constraints: Cannot take unpaid leave at short notice because of court dates
Will not push her mother into a move she does not accept
Keeps client confidentiality strictly; no case details outside the firm
Cannot afford a care home upgrade for her mother without family contribution
sensitive: Guilt about living two hundred miles from her mother
Worries she is better at holding other families' arguments than her own

disclosure_policy.t1_after_signal: Mother falls, kitchen delay, son plays chess
disclosure_policy.t2_after_trust: Family disagreement about Mum, guilt, tiredness
disclosure_policy.never: Client details, case files, family medical information
